questions.question: Does the proposed temperature-dependent reduction in stacking fault energy quantitatively drive the fcc-to-hcp transition in CoCrFeMnNi at high pressure, and what is the threshold temperature below which this mechanism dominates?
questions.rationale: Answering this confirms if the mechanism of SFE reduction is the primary driver or a secondary effect, changing how researchers design heat treatments to stabilize metastable phases.
questions.decision_use: Selects between kinetic barrier reduction strategies and thermodynamic driving force strategies for phase engineering.
answer_requirements: Measure stacking fault energy as a function of temperature (e.g., via MD simulations or mechanical testing) and correlate with critical transition temperatures observed in diffraction.
Compare the observed temperature trend against the predicted SFE reduction curve.
evidence_spans: This observation indicates that the stacking fault energy may diminish with decreasing temperature, which could facilitate the sliding needed for a displacive phase transition from fcc to hcp

The hcp structure can be readily obtained locally from a fcc structure by introducing stacking faults. And it can be easily realized in the current HEA because recent experiment [41] and simulations [37] [41] have confirmed that it indeed has a low staking fault energy of ∼20 mJ m −2

questions.question: At what specific pressure and temperature conditions does the hcp phase in CoCrFeMnNi become thermodynamically unstable relative to the fcc phase, defining the boundary of the proposed phase diagram?
questions.rationale: Defining the exact boundary allows for the precise synthesis of either pure hcp or controlled fcc/hcp composites, which is currently only empirically known.
questions.decision_use: Determines the processing window (P, T) for retaining the metastable hcp phase for high-strength applications.
answer_requirements: Construct a continuous P-T phase diagram by mapping the transition temperatures (Tc) at multiple pressures (P) up to the stability limit.
Identify the intersection point where the free energy difference between fcc and hcp changes sign.
evidence_spans: Based on four critical transition temperatures determined at different pressures, a boundary is proposed in Fig. 3b .
and almost completely transformed back to fcc when heated up to 723 K ( Supplementary Fig. 5 ).

questions.question: What is the minimum pressure required to initiate the fcc-to-hcp transition in CoCrFeMnNi under isothermal conditions, and does this pressure threshold remain constant for samples with different initial grain sizes?
questions.rationale: Knowing if microstructure (grain size) affects the transition pressure is critical for scaling up synthesis; if it does, grain refinement becomes a necessary pre-processing step.
questions.decision_use: Informs whether post-synthesis heat treatment or grain refinement is required to lower the pressure threshold for hcp synthesis.
answer_requirements: Perform in situ high-pressure XRD on samples with systematically varied grain sizes.
Measure the onset pressure of new hcp diffraction peaks for each grain size variant.
evidence_spans: Once the pressure approaches 22.1 GPa, extra diffraction peaks beside the (111) peak of fcc appeared (indicated by red triangles in Fig. 1c ), suggesting the occurrence of a phase transition.
The polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp unveiled in this work demonstrates that high-pressure can help overcome the kinetic barrier between hcp and fcc HEAs.

questions.question: How does the fraction of retained hcp phase in decompressed CoCrFeMnNi composites scale with the maximum applied pressure, and is this relationship linear up to 41 GPa?
questions.rationale: Establishing the quantitative relationship between peak pressure and final phase fraction is essential for designing composites with specific mechanical properties.
questions.decision_use: Allows precise tuning of the fcc/hcp ratio for targeted strength-ductility combinations.
answer_requirements: Systematically compress samples to varying pressures (22, 25, 28, 31, 34, 37, 41 GPa), decompress, and quantify phase fractions via Rietveld refinement of XRD patterns.
Plot phase fraction versus maximum pressure to determine the functional form.
evidence_spans: Decompression from different maximum pressures between ∼22 and ∼41 GPa in our repeated experiments successfully obtains fcc / hcp composites with tunable fractions after pressure release.
